Series::rrelu¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::rrelu(
    double lower = 0.125,
    double upper = 0.3333333333333333,
    bool training = false) const
Series& Series::rrelu_(bool training) const

Randomized Or Deterministic Negative Slopes¶

rrelu() leaves positive elements unchanged and multiplies each non-positive element by a slope. The source of that slope depends on training:

  • with training=false, every non-positive lane uses the deterministic midpoint (lower + upper) / 2;

  • with training=true, every non-positive lane receives its own independent slope sampled uniformly from the closed numeric interval bounded by lower and upper.

Evaluation mode is therefore an ordinary leaky rectifier with a fixed slope. Training mode injects multiplicative noise only into the non-positive branch. This split lets training use randomized slopes while inference remains stable and reproducible.

lower and upper must be finite and ordered, but they need not be positive. A negative interval is meaningful: multiplying a negative input by a negative slope produces a positive output. Most activation use chooses a non-negative interval, but the method enforces ordering rather than imposing that policy.

Shape, Dtype, And Randomness¶

  • The result has the same shape, dtype, and platform as the receiver.

  • The receiver must have a floating-point dtype. Integer, Boolean, and complex receivers are rejected rather than silently changing the sampling domain.

  • Positive lanes do not consume their sampled slope semantically; their output and derivative are exactly the input and one.

  • The method is out of place and does not mutate the receiver.

  • Set the shared Pluss random seed before a training call when reproducible examples or experiments are required. Re-seeding resets the stream.

Reverse Mode¶

The exact slopes realized during the training forward pass are retained by its single reverse node. A negative lane therefore receives the same slope in reverse; backward never resamples. Evaluation mode uses the deterministic midpoint in both directions. At zero the non-positive branch applies.

In-Place Form¶

rrelu_() is the in-place sibling of rrelu(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — rrelu_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, 0.0, 2.0});

// training=false uses the deterministic eval-mode slope
// (the midpoint of [lower, upper]), not a random draw.
x.rrelu_(false);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.45833333, 0, 2]

Examples¶

1. Use deterministic defaults for evaluation¶

const auto x = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.rrelu());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.6875, -0.2292, 0.0000, 1.0000, 3.0000]

The default midpoint is (0.125 + 1/3) / 2, approximately 0.2291667. Because training defaults to false, repeated calls produce the same values.

2. Choose a custom evaluation interval¶

const auto x = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.rrelu(0.2, 0.4, false));

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.9000, -0.3000, 0.0000, 1.0000, 3.0000]

Evaluation uses midpoint 0.3; it does not draw a random value from the interval.

3. Ordered negative bounds are valid¶

const auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 2.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.rrelu(-0.4, -0.2, false));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.6000, 0.3000, 0.0000, 2.0000]

The midpoint is -0.3. This example is mathematically valid, although a positive negative-branch slope is the usual activation policy.

4. Seed a training-mode draw¶

pluss::rng_seed(20260928);
const auto x = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.rrelu(0.2, 0.4, true));

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.0932, -0.2805, 0.0000, 1.0000, 3.0000]

Each of the first three lanes receives an independent slope in [0.2, 0.4]. The positive lanes remain exact identities.

5. Reverse mode reuses the realized slopes¶

pluss::rng_seed(20260928);
auto x = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.rrelu(0.2, 0.4, true).sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[0.3644, 0.2805, 0.2320, 1.0000, 1.0000]

For example, -3 * 0.3644 gives the first forward value -1.0932 after rounding. The reverse slope is the same draw, including at zero where the output alone cannot reveal it.

6. Reject reversed bounds¶

try {
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({-1.0, 1.0});
  (void)x.rrelu(0.5, 0.1, true);
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::cout << error.what() << '\n';
}

Output¶

rrelu: expected finite bounds with lower <= upper

NaN and infinite bounds fail the same finite-interval validation.

7. Reject non-floating receivers¶

try {
  (void)pluss::make_series({-2, 1}).rrelu();
} catch (const std::exception& error) {
  std::cout << error.what() << '\n';
}

Output¶

rrelu: input must have a floating-point dtype

Explicitly convert an integer Series when floating randomized activation is intended.

Performance¶

Evaluation mode is a deterministic elementwise activation. Training mode also generates one slope per lane and retains that slope Series for reverse mode. It is therefore more expensive in both bandwidth and saved state. Do not use training=true for inference when the randomized behavior is unwanted.

See Also¶

  • leaky_relu() accepts one deterministic negative slope.

  • relu() uses a zero negative slope.

  • uniform_() fills an existing Series from a uniform distribution.
